title: Reverse a linked list — iterative (prev/curr/next) and recursive.
shortTitle: Reverse a Linked List — Iterative (prev/curr/next) and Recursive

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing a singly linked list makes the last node the new head and flips every next pointer to point backward. The iterative method walks the list with three references, previous, current, and next, rewiring each node's link as it goes, in O(n) time and O(1) space. The recursive method reverses the rest of the list first and then fixes the current node's link, in O(n) time and O(n) stack space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India stores a chain of transactions oldest-to-newest and wants to display it newest-to-oldest. Rajesh walks the chain and flips each arrow to point to the node he just came from, keeping a note of the previous node, the current node, and the next node so he never loses the rest of the chain while flipping.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flip each next pointer to the previous node, tracking previous, current, and next so the remaining list is never lost.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing a singly linked list makes the last node the new head and flips every next pointer to point backward. The iterative method walks the list with three references, previous, current, and next, rewiring each node's link as it goes, in O(n) time and O(1) space. The recursive method reverses the rest of the list first and then fixes the current node's link, in O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India stores a chain of transactions oldest-to-newest and wants to display it newest-to-oldest. Rajesh walks the chain and flips each arrow to point to the node he just came from, keeping a note of the previous node, the current node, and the next node so he never loses the rest of the chain while flipping.

**One line to remember:** Flip each next pointer to the previous node, tracking previous, current, and next so the remaining list is never lost.

sections.s2_technical:
The iterative approach uses three references. Start `prev = null` and `curr = head`. In a loop while `curr != null`: save `next = curr.next`, set `curr.next = prev` to flip the link, then advance `prev = curr` and `curr = next`. When the loop ends, `prev` is the new head. Saving `next` before flipping is essential, because once `curr.next` is overwritten the rest of the list would be unreachable otherwise.

A code snippet on a transaction list: `Node reverse(Node head) { Node prev = null, curr = head; while (curr != null) { Node next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next; } return prev; }`. Each node is visited once and only pointers change, so it is linear time and constant space.

The recursive approach reverses from the tail. If the list is empty or a single node, return it. Otherwise recurse on `head.next` to reverse the remainder, which returns the new head; then set `head.next.next = head` to make the next node point back to the current one, and set `head.next = null` to terminate. A code snippet: `Node reverseRec(Node head) { if (head == null || head.next == null) return head; Node newHead = reverseRec(head.next); head.next.next = head; head.next = null; return newHead; }`.

The two differ in space. The iterative version uses constant extra memory, while the recursive version uses stack frames proportional to the list length, which can overflow on very long lists. A senior nuance is that the recursive rewiring line `head.next.next = head` is the crux: after the rest is reversed, the original successor of the current node must point back to it. Interviewers often ask for both, and the iterative one is preferred in production precisely because it avoids deep recursion on large lists.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps a customer's transaction chain in chronological order but the statement view must show newest first, so the service reverses the linked list. This is exactly how linked-list reversal works — every next pointer is flipped so traversal runs the other way.

Problem 2 — Statements can be long, so the production path uses the iterative constant-space reversal to avoid deep recursion, while the recursive version is kept for clarity and small lists.

The code shows a `StatementOrderService` with both `reverseIterative` and `reverseRecursive`, a demo reversing a transaction list, and the printed order.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the transaction list T1, T2, T3, T4.

Step 1: Iterative. prev is null, curr is T1. Save next as T2, flip T1's next to null, advance prev to T1 and curr to T2. The reversed part so far is just T1 pointing to null.

Step 2: Save next as T3, flip T2's next to T1, advance prev to T2 and curr to T3. The reversed part is T2 pointing to T1.

Step 3: Save next as T4, flip T3's next to T2, advance prev to T3 and curr to T4. Then save next as null, flip T4's next to T3, advance prev to T4 and curr to null. The loop ends and prev is T4, the new head. The list reads T4, T3, T2, T1.

Step 4: Recursive on a fresh T1 to T4. The calls descend until the base case returns T4 as the new head. Unwinding, T3's successor T4 is made to point back to T3, then T3's forward link is nulled; similarly T2 and T1 are rewired on the way back up.

Step 5: Both methods produce the same reversed chain T4 to T1, shown as the newest-first statement order.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Iterative reversed: T4 -> T3 -> T2 -> T1
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Recursive reversed: T4 -> T3 -> T2 -> T1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing a singly linked list means making the last node the new head and flipping every next pointer to point backward, and I know both the iterative and recursive ways. The iterative method walks the list with three references: previous, current, and next. On each step I first save the current node's next so I do not lose the rest of the list, then I flip the current node's link to point at the previous node, and finally I advance previous and current forward. When current runs off the end, previous is the new head. This is linear time and uses only constant extra memory.

Saving the next reference before flipping is the detail that matters most in the iterative version. The moment I overwrite the current node's next to point backward, the forward link to the remainder is gone, so if I had not stored it first the rest of the list would be unreachable.

The recursive method reverses from the tail. I recurse to reverse everything after the head, which hands back the new head, then I set the current node's original successor to point back at the current node and null the current node's forward link. The crucial line is making the successor point back, because after the rest is reversed that successor is now behind the current node. The recursive version is elegant but uses stack space proportional to the list length, so on very long lists it risks a stack overflow, which is why I prefer the iterative constant-space version in production.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the statement service. Transactions were stored oldest first, but the statement view had to show newest first, so I reversed the linked list, using the iterative method on the long production lists to avoid deep recursion and keeping the recursive version for clarity and small cases. Explaining both methods, the save-next rule in the iterative version, the successor-rewiring line in the recursive version, and the space trade-off shows the interviewer I understand linked-list pointer manipulation thoroughly.
